spans.text: The tower stood on the highest hill in the county and there was nothing else on the hill at all.

That was the first thing anybody said about it and it was the thing they went on saying for two hundred years. It stood on the bare top with the grass going away from it in every direction, and in a wind it was the only object between the man standing at the bottom of it and the sky, and men who had grown up in that valley did not care for it and could not entirely have said why.

It was not a fine building. It had been put up in a hurry by a man with money and no patience, and the stone had come off the hill it stood on, and the courses were not true. There was a door at the bottom. There were four narrow windows going up. At the top there was a room.

The room at the top had windows on all sides and a flat lead roof above it, and on the night this happened it had three candles burning in it and one man, and the man had been in it since about four in the afternoon.
The boy came up at nine with the water.

He came up because he always came up at nine with the water, and because the stair was ninety-one steps and the man was fifty-four and had stopped doing it himself in about the spring. The boy was eleven. His name was Bright and his father was Bright and the two of them between them had the hill, the hanger and the west park, and they had had it for as long as anybody bothered to remember.
He put the can down inside the door and waited to be noticed, which took some while.

The man was at the long bench under the north windows with his back to the room. There was a great deal on that bench. There was a small brick furnace at the far end of it with the fire in it damped down to almost nothing, and a bowl of sand, and a rack of files, and a wooden box with about forty compartments in it, and a stone mortar, and eleven glass jars with paper labels tied on with string.
Bright,
said the man, without turning round.
Sir.
How is the wind.
It has gone round to the west,
said the boy.
It has been west since about seven.
Is it going to rain.
My father says not before Thursday.
Your father is right more often than the almanack,
said the man,
which I have paid four shillings a year for since I came here, and I shall go on paying it, because a man who only takes advice that is correct learns nothing about advice.
The boy did not know what to do with that and said nothing, which was generally the right answer.
The man turned round on his stool.

He was not an impressive figure and he knew it and had made his peace with it a long way back. He was heavy about the middle. He had a wide plain face and bad teeth and hands that were ruined, burned across the backs in three places and one thumbnail gone black and staying black. He wore an apron over good clothes and had done so long enough that the good clothes underneath had stopped being good.

He had bought his title eleven years before from a man in London who had needed the money more than he had needed the title, and he had paid a great deal for it, and he had never once in eleven years managed to say the word lord about himself out loud without something going wrong in his face.
Light the third one,
he said.
There are three, sir.
There are two lit and one not. Look at it properly.
The boy looked at it properly. The third candle was in its stick at the far left end of the bench and it had gone out at some point in the evening and neither of them had noticed.
He lit it off the second one.
Now,
said the man.
Put your hand out over the bench.
The boy put his hand out over the bench.
What do you see.
My hand.
What do you not see.

The boy looked. It took him about four seconds and he got there without help, and the man watched him get there and did not hurry him, which was the thing about the man that the boy remembered for the rest of his life and told his own children about, and which was the reason the Brights stayed on that estate for a hundred and ninety years.
There is no shadow,
the boy said.
There is no shadow.
There ought to be a shadow.
There ought to be three,
said the man,

and there are three, and each one falls where another candle is throwing light, and so between them they have cancelled the thing out. That is the whole of it. That is why there are three and not two, and it is not a mystery and it is not learning, it is arithmetic about candles, and it costs me a third more in wax.
He turned back to the bench.

A man doing fine work with two candles is working in his own shadow and does not know it. He thinks his eyes are going. Mine are not going. I have had that argument with myself twice this year and won it both times.
What he was doing at the bench, on that night, in the middle of that summer, was grinding.

He had been grinding for six weeks. He had a shallow copper dish and a quantity of grey grit and a quantity of water, and in the dish, under the grit and the water, there was a piece of something about the size of a walnut, and he had been taking it down a very little at a time with his thumb going round in a circle, and stopping to look, and going round again.
He had got it out of the ground himself in April.

That was a thing he was going to be extremely particular about later, in the volumes, and he was particular about it that night to a boy who had not asked. He had got it out of the ground himself, on this hill, at a depth of about nine feet, out of a seam he had opened with two men and a pick because a seam of that kind had been described to him in a letter from a Cornishman and he had wanted to see one. He had brought up a good deal of rock. Most of it had been nothing. One piece had not been nothing.
You found it,
said the boy.
I found it.
Then it is a found thing.
It was a found thing in April.
The man went on grinding and did not look up.

It has had six weeks of me since then. Every night since the fourteenth of May and most of the afternoons. It has been heated four times and quenched three and it has been in acid twice and it has lost about a third of what it weighed when it came up.
He stopped, and put his thumb on the edge of the dish, and looked at the water going still.
Now tell me what it is.
The boy thought about it.
Still a found thing,
he said.
But less.
The man laughed, which he did not do much, and it went on a bit longer than the joke deserved.
That is better than anything I have written down about it,
he said.
I have written four pages on that question and I have not got as far as still a found thing, but less.
There is one more thing about that bench and it is the thing the volumes do not have.

He wrote down everything. That was the whole of his method and it was the only thing about him that any scholar ever admired. He wrote down the weather and the hour and the weight before and the weight after. He wrote down his failures in the same hand and at the same length as his successes, which almost nobody did then and not many do now.
He did not write down what the four heatings cost.

The first of them had taken the skin off the back of his left hand from the knuckle to the wrist, in April, and he had gone down the ninety-one steps afterward and walked four miles in the dark rather than send for anybody, and had come back up at first light and done the second one. The third had done the thumb. The fourth had done something that did not show at all and that he noticed in his chest for eleven days afterward and stopped noticing, or said he had.
None of that is in Volume One. Volume One for that fortnight has the weather, the hours, the weights and the word proceeded, six times.
The boy carrying the water saw the hand in April and asked about it once.
Sir, your hand.
Yes.
Ought that to be seen to.
It has been seen to,
said the man, who had put a wet rag on it in the dark four miles from anywhere and had then walked home.
Put the can down.
My mother has a salve for a burn. It is mostly goose grease and it is not much to look at.

Your mother’s salve is very likely better than anything I should be given for eight shillings in this county, and I am not going to have it, and I would rather not say why, and you are not to tell her I refused it.
The boy put the can down.
No, sir.
Good lad. Go down.
He did not ask again, because he was eleven and had been well brought up, and because he had heard, without being able to name it, that the refusing had not been about the salve.
At about eleven he sent the boy down.

He did it in the way he did everything, which was abruptly and without any of the softening that other men put round the edges of an instruction, and the boy had long since stopped minding it and had begun, without noticing, to do it himself.
Go down. Tell your father the wind is west and I want the door wedged and not barred.
Yes, sir.
And Bright.
The boy stopped on the stair.
You are not to come up in the morning,
said the man.
Not at seven and not at nine. If I want water I shall come down for it. Tell your father that as well and tell him I said it twice.

The boy went down the ninety-one steps in the dark, because he had gone down them in the dark two hundred times and did not need a light for it, and at the bottom he wedged the door and did not bar it and went home across the hill in a west wind.

He was eleven. He did not think anything at all about the instruction, and he did not think anything about it the following morning either, and it was about four years before it occurred to him that there was only one reason a man tells you twice not to come up.
The man worked on.
He took it out of the dish at some time after midnight and dried it on a linen rag and put it on the bench in the light of the three candles and looked at it.

It was not much to look at. It was about the size of a hazelnut by then and it was a dull unpromising grey with a slight warmth in the grey, and it had six faces on it now where in April it had had none, and the faces were not good. Two of them were true and the rest were near enough and one was frankly bad. He had put them there himself with a file and a copper dish and six weeks, and he knew exactly which of them he had done well and which he had rushed, and he was not a man who lied to himself about work.
He wrote for about forty minutes.

Then he did the thing he had been intending to do since the fourteenth of May and had not done, and had put off on four separate evenings for four separate reasons, all of which he had written down and none of which had been the real one.
He put out two of the candles.

He did it deliberately and in order, the third one first and then the second, and he did it with his fingers and not a snuffer, and he sat in the dark at the bench with one candle burning at his right hand and the piece of stone in front of him on the linen rag.
Then he put his hand over the last candle.
What happened next is the sentence the family could never agree about.

There were, in the end, three versions of it, and they were all in the house by the time there were great-aunts in it to tell them, and each of the three was told with complete confidence by somebody who had it from somebody who had been alive at the time.
In one of them he found something.
In another he made something.

In the third, which was the one the children liked best and which was the least use to anybody, he did both, and the two were not different things at all, and the whole question was a foolish one got up by people who had never made anything themselves.

What is certain, because it is in his own hand in the first of the twenty volumes, is that he was still at the bench when it got light, that he had not eaten, and that he did not go down for water at seven or at nine, and that at some point in the early part of that morning he wrote a single line and then left three quarters of the page blank underneath it, which he never did, before or after, in twenty volumes and forty-one years.
The line was this.

I have to decide what to call it, and I find that I would rather not, because the moment I call it a thing I have found, I am telling a lie, and the moment I call it a thing I have made, I am telling a different one.
He did not fill in the rest of the page.

The tower stood on the highest hill in the county with the door wedged and not barred, and there was nothing else on the hill at all, and below it, four miles off across the west park, there was no house yet, and would not be one for another twenty-six years.
